title: Shout It Out
summary: Publish an event once and let any number of services react — fan-out, decoupling, replayable logs, ordering per key and consumer groups.

goals.text: See how direct calls couple a service to everything downstream
Fan out events to independent subscribers
Replay history from an event log

steps.title: Checkout calls everyone
body: Bramble sells houseplants online. When a shopper checks out, the Orders service charges the card and then, one by one, asks Email to send a receipt, Inventory to reserve stock, Analytics to record the sale and Loyalty to add points.
Each call is quick on its own, but they add up: the shopper stares at a spinner for over a second while Orders runs errands.

steps.title: A receipt takes down checkout
body: The email provider has an outage. Orders waits for its 5-second timeout, then treats the whole checkout as failed. Shoppers with full baskets and valid cards can't buy anything.
This is temporal coupling: Orders can only succeed when every service it calls is up at that same moment. The more services in the chain, the more often one of them isn't.

card.title: Email is down
lines: the email provider times out after 5 s
! the order fails — the plants were in stock

steps.title: Everyone's changes land in Orders
body: Marketing wants a free gift on a customer's first order. That's a new service — and, with direct calls, another change to Orders: new client code, new error handling, another redeploy of the most critical service in the company.
Orders has become the place where every team's feature has to be wired in.

steps.title: Announce it, don't arrange it
body: Flip the arrows. Orders still charges the card synchronously (it must know the payment worked), then publishes one event — OrderPlaced — to a topic and replies to the shopper.
Every interested service subscribes to the topic and gets its own copy. This is publish/subscribe: the publisher states a fact; subscribers decide what to do about it.

callout.text: An event is a fact in the past tense (“order placed”), not a command (“send email”). The publisher doesn't care who reacts.

steps.title: New listener, zero changes
body: The Gift team creates their own subscription and starts receiving OrderPlaced events. Orders isn't touched or redeployed. This fan-out is the payoff of decoupling: adding a consumer costs the publisher nothing.

steps.title: One subscriber down, nobody else cares
body: The email provider fails again. This time checkout doesn't notice: Email's subscription simply keeps collecting events — 1,200 receipts waiting — while Inventory, Analytics, Loyalty and Gift carry on.
When Email recovers it works through the pile. Receipts arrive late, but none are lost and no sale was refused.
changes: + Email's copies pile up in its subscription

steps.title: Keep the events, rewind at will
body: Many systems store events in an append-only event log kept for days or forever. Consumers don't remove events; each one tracks an offset — how far it has read.
That makes history reusable: a brand-new Analytics v2 can start at offset 0 and rebuild its numbers from every order ever placed, while Email catches up from where it stopped.
changes: ~ Analytics v2 replays from the start

card.title: A log, not a mailbox
lines: each reader keeps its own bookmark

steps.title: Order, but only per key
body: One log can't absorb unlimited traffic, so it's split into partitions read in parallel. Order is only guaranteed inside a partition.

So pick a partition key. Keying by order id sends every event about order 881 to the same partition, so Inventory never sees “Refunded” before “Placed”. Events of different orders may interleave, which is fine.

callout.text: A hot key (one huge customer) lands on one partition and can't be spread. Choose keys with many, evenly busy values.

card.title: Key = order id
lines: = one order's events stay in order
! no order promised across P0, P1, P2

steps.title: Share the work, not the events
body: Inventory runs three instances. They join one consumer group: the log assigns each partition to exactly one member, so each event is handled once by the group and order per partition holds.
Analytics is a different group, so it still receives every event. Inside a group: load-sharing. Across groups: broadcast.

steps.title: The price of not waiting
body: Checkout is fast because it no longer waits — which means the rest happens eventually. A shopper may look for loyalty points a few seconds too early.

And the flow is harder to see: no single function shows what happens after a sale. You need event schemas treated as contracts, tracing across consumers, and dead-letter handling for events a subscriber can't process.

card.title: Done… eventually
lines: # events are contracts: version the schema

steps.title: Say it once, let others listen
body:
• Keep the calls you truly need answers from (payment) synchronous; publish the rest as events.
  • Pub/sub fans one event out to any number of independent subscribers.
  • A slow or broken subscriber only delays itself.
  • Event logs keep history: consumers track offsets and can replay.
  • Order holds per partition — key events by the entity they describe.
  • Consumer groups share partitions; separate groups each get everything.
